opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so my advisor was Gerard 't Hooft, and for a long time now he's been pursuing what he calls the cellular automaton interpretation of quantum mechanics. The basic idea is that underneath quantum mechanics there's a deterministic system, something like a cellular automaton at the Planck scale, and the quantum description we use is just an effective, statistical way of talking about it. So the probabilities aren't fundamental; they come from our ignorance about the underlying states.

I have a lot of sympathy for the motivation. Gerard has always been bothered that quantum mechanics, as we usually present it, works perfectly as a calculational machine but doesn't really tell you what is *happening*. The measurement problem, the collapse of the wave function: these things are swept under the rug, and he refuses to sweep them. I really admire that. It takes some courage, when you've already won a Nobel Prize for very mainstream work, to go after something most of your colleagues think is a lost cause.

The big obstacle, of course, is Bell's theorem. If you want a local deterministic theory underneath, you run into the Bell inequality violations we see in experiments. Gerard's answer is superdeterminism: the settings experimenters choose aren't truly independent of the hidden variables, because everything, including the experimenter's brain, is part of the same deterministic evolution from the initial conditions. A lot of physicists find that deeply unsatisfying, almost like giving up on science, because it seems to undermine the idea of a free, controlled experiment. Gerard would say that's a prejudice, not a theorem.

Where do I land? I think it's a legitimate research program, and I'm glad someone of his caliber is pursuing it, even if it hasn't yet produced a prediction that would distinguish it from standard quantum mechanics. That's really the test. And honestly, it has influenced how I think. Coming into machine learning, I've always been interested in the link between physics and computation, the idea that maybe the universe is, at some level, a kind of computation. Gerard's cellular automaton picture is one very concrete version of that. So even if I'm agnostic about whether he's right, the spirit of it, asking what the computational substrate of reality is, has stayed with me.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the cellular automaton theory and its obstacles, but does not contrast difficulty understanding it with the relative simplicity of its mathematics.

r002.rationale: The response says Welling sympathizes with the goal of explaining what is happening, but does not express his own desire to understand quantum mechanics in ordinary, intuitive terms.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, my PhD advisor was Gerard 't Hooft, who won the Nobel Prize in 1999 for his work on the Standard Model, and for the last twenty-odd years he's been working on what he calls the cellular automaton interpretation of quantum mechanics. The basic idea is that underneath quantum mechanics there is actually a deterministic theory, something like a cellular automaton running at the Planck scale, and that the probabilistic, superposition-type behavior we see is an emergent description of that underlying deterministic dynamics. So it's a kind of hidden variable theory, in the spirit of what Einstein hoped for, except he tries to get around Bell's theorem through what people call superdeterminism.

I have a lot of respect for it, and honestly a lot of affection, because this is a man who is not afraid to be in the minority. Most of the physics community thinks it's a dead end, and he knows that, and he keeps going anyway because he thinks the question is too important to leave alone. I find that admirable. I was his student at the time he was starting to move in this direction, and what I remember is that he was always asking the questions that other people considered settled. That attitude shaped me more than any specific result did.

Now, do I think he's right? I honestly don't know, and I'm not a working physicist anymore, so I should be a bit humble here. My intuition is that superdeterminism is a very high price to pay. You have to give up the idea that the experimenter's choices are independent of the system being measured, and that makes it hard to do science in the usual sense. On the other hand, I spend my days now thinking about machine learning, and one thing you learn there is that very simple deterministic rules can produce behavior that looks completely random and incredibly rich. So the idea that quantum mechanics could be an effective theory on top of something simpler and discrete doesn't seem crazy to me at all. In fact, the way we think about emergence in deep learning, where you have these very simple update rules and complex behavior comes out, has a bit of the same flavor.

What I find interesting is that his program is really about understanding, not just prediction. Quantum mechanics predicts perfectly well, nobody disputes that. The question he's asking is whether there's a story that a human can actually hold in their head about what's going on. And I think that's a legitimate scientific goal, even if the community has decided it's not fashionable. We're seeing a similar tension in AI now, where we have models that work extremely well and we don't understand them, and there's a debate about whether understanding even matters. So in a funny way his stubbornness looks more relevant to me now than it did when I was a student.

r002.rationale: Welling endorses the goal of finding a story about quantum mechanics that a person can hold in their head, expressing a preference for an intuitive understanding.

astra-6.text: I think it’s a very worthwhile pursuit. Quantum mechanics is extraordinarily successful at predicting what we observe, but that doesn’t mean we have a satisfying understanding of what’s underneath it. My advisor was willing to question assumptions that most people take for granted, and I admire that independence of thought. Of course, wanting a more understandable theory doesn’t make it correct. The challenge is to turn that intuition into something precise that reproduces what we already know and, ideally, gives us something new to test.

sol-6.1.text: I think the ambition is a very worthwhile one. Quantum mechanics is extraordinarily successful at making predictions, but that doesn’t necessarily mean we have an intuitive understanding of what it’s telling us about the world. Trying to find a clearer underlying picture is a legitimate scientific question. The hard part is turning that picture into something you can test. So I’d distinguish between appreciating the ambition and being convinced by a particular proposal.
